paragraphs: Two men were talking. One was a physician.
“I sent for you, Doctor,” said the other, “but I don’t think you can do me any good. Perhaps you can recommend a specialist in mental illness. I think I’m a little mad.”
“You look all right,” the physician said.
“You can judge for yourself—I have hallucinations. Every night I wake and see a big black Newfoundland dog with one white front paw in my room, watching me intently.”
“You say you wake. Are you certain of that? ‘Hallucinations’ are sometimes only dreams.”

“Oh, I certainly wake. Sometimes I lie still for a long time, watching the dog as intently as it watches me. I always leave the light on. When I can’t bear it any longer, I sit up in bed—and there’s nothing there!”
“Hmm, hmm—what expression does the animal have?”

“It looks sinister to me. Of course, I know that, except in art, an animal’s face at rest always has the same expression. But this isn’t a real animal. Newfoundland dogs usually look quite gentle, you know. What’s the matter with this one?”
“Really, my diagnosis would be worthless. I’m not going to treat the dog.”

The physician laughed at his own joke, but watched his patient closely from the corner of his eye. After a moment he said, “Fleming, your description of the animal matches the dog that belonged to the late Atwell Barton.”

Fleming half rose from his chair, sat down again, and visibly tried to look indifferent. “I remember Barton,” he said. “I believe he was—it was reported that—wasn’t there something suspicious about his death?”

Looking directly into his patient’s eyes now, the physician said, “Three years ago, the body of your old enemy, Atwell Barton, was found in the woods near his house and yours. He had been stabbed to death. No one has been arrested. There was no clue. Some of us had ‘theories.’ I had one. Have you?”

“Me? Why, bless you, what could I know about it? You remember that I left for Europe almost immediately afterwards—a considerable time afterwards. You can hardly expect me to have worked out a ‘theory’ in the few weeks since I returned. In fact, I haven’t given the matter a thought. What about his dog?”
“It was the first to find the body. It starved to death on his grave.”

We do not know the unyielding law behind coincidences. Staley Fleming did not know it, or perhaps he would not have leapt to his feet when the night wind carried the long, wailing howl of a distant dog through the open window. He strode back and forth across the room several times under the physician’s steady gaze. Then he suddenly faced him and almost shouted, “What has any of this to do with my trouble, Dr. Halderman? You’ve forgotten why you were sent for.”

The physician rose, laid a hand on his patient’s arm, and said gently, “Forgive me. I can’t diagnose your condition straight away—perhaps tomorrow. Please go to bed and leave your door unlocked. I’ll spend the night here with your books. Can you call me without getting up?”
“Yes, there’s an electric bell.”
“Good. If anything disturbs you, press the button without sitting up. Good night.”

Settled comfortably in an armchair, the physician stared into the glowing coals and thought deeply for a long time. Apparently, however, his thoughts led nowhere. He often got up, opened a door leading to the staircase, and listened intently before returning to his seat. Eventually he fell asleep. When he woke, it was past midnight. He stirred the dying fire, picked up a book from the table beside him, and looked at its title. It was Denneker’s “Meditations.” He opened it at random and began to read:

“Since God has decreed that all flesh has a spirit, and through it takes on spiritual powers, the spirit also has the powers of the flesh—even after leaving the body and living separately. Many acts of violence committed by ghosts and restless spirits of the dead show this. Some say that humanity is not alone in this, and that animals have the same inclination towards evil, and—”

His reading was interrupted by a shaking of the house, as though something heavy had fallen. He threw down the book, rushed from the room, and ran upstairs to Fleming’s bedroom. He tried the door, but, contrary to his instructions, it was locked. He drove his shoulder against it so forcefully that it gave way. On the floor near the disordered bed lay Fleming in his nightclothes, gasping out his life.
The physician lifted the dying man’s head from the floor and saw a wound in his throat. “I should have thought of this,” he said, believing it was suicide.
After the man died, an examination revealed the unmistakable marks of an animal’s fangs that had sunk deep into his jugular vein.
But there was no animal.
